topic: building a garden sauna from a flat-pack kit over one weekend

provenance.author: glowny-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is panel, screw and schedule arithmetic on the same kit with closed task questions, base is an exploratory build-order dialogue. Grounded external referent: the heater, introduced in turn 0 (nervous about it, in its crate) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (crate, shed, rating plate, back left corner).

a: The sauna kit arrived as six wall panels, and their weights need sorting before we carry them.
The two long panels weigh forty kilograms each, and the two short panels weigh twenty-five each.
The front panel with the door cut-out weighs thirty kilograms on the delivery sheet.
The gable panel is the lightest of the six at twenty kilograms exactly.
Sort the six panels from heaviest to lightest and give a running total after each one.
How many kilograms do all six panels come to at the end of that list?
base: Our garden sauna kit arrived on Friday, and the slab we poured last month is cured and level.
The wall panels are stacked under a tarp, and the roof boards lean against the fence.
The heater came in its own crate, and it is the one part we are nervous about.
We have two clear days, one helper, and no wish to lift anything twice.
The manual shows the finished building but says almost nothing about the order of the work.
Where would you start on the first morning so the weekend does not fall apart?

a: Sorted heaviest to lightest, the two long panels come first at forty kilograms apiece.
The running total stands at eighty kilograms once both long panels are on the list.
The front panel brings the total to one hundred ten, and the short panels to one hundred sixty.
The gable panel closes the list and lifts the figure to one hundred eighty kilograms.
Does that final figure of one hundred eighty match the weight printed on the delivery sheet?
base: Start with the floor frame, because every wall panel takes its line from that first rectangle.
Check the slab with a straight edge before any timber goes down on it.
Walls go up in pairs, and the door panel goes in last so the opening stays square.
The heater stays in its crate until the roof is on and the room is weather tight.
Have you checked whether the slab sits level along both diagonals, not just the edges?

a: Now count the fixings, because the kit lists three packs of screws in different lengths.
The long pack holds one hundred twenty screws, the middle pack eighty, and the short pack sixty.
Each wall panel needs eighteen long screws and the roof needs forty of the middle length.
Set aside the screws for the six walls and tell me what remains in the long pack.
How many long screws are left over once all six wall panels are fixed down?
base: The slab passed the straight edge along both diagonals, so the floor frame can go straight down.
The heater crate is in the shed, and the packing list says the stones travel inside the firebox.
One long wall panel has taken a bow from lying under the tarp through the wet spring.
We would rather not order a new panel this late in the season.
Can a bowed panel be pulled straight while it is screwed to the frame?

a: Six wall panels at eighteen long screws each takes one hundred eight from the long pack.
That leaves twelve long screws spare once every wall panel is fixed to the frame.
The roof takes forty middle screws and leaves forty in that pack for the trims.
The short pack stays untouched at sixty until the benches go in on day two.
Do the twelve spare long screws cover the two corner braces at five screws each?
base: A bow of a few millimetres will pull straight, so screw the good edge first and work across.
Fit that panel between two straight ones and let the frame do the holding for you.
The manual also gives clearance distances, and those decide the standing corner before anything else.
Keep the heater clear of the walls by the distances printed on its rating plate.
Which corner of the room does the flue leave from in the kit drawings?

a: One correction before the next step: the front panel weighs thirty-four kilograms, not thirty.
Rework the running totals from the front panel onward and leave the earlier figures alone.
Then give the new grand total for all six wall panels together.
The trailer we hired is rated to carry two hundred kilograms in one trip.
Does the corrected total for the six panels still sit under that trailer rating?
base: The drawings put the flue in the back left corner, straight up through the roof panel.
That corner also holds the biggest clearance box drawn anywhere on the plan.
So the heater will stand in back left, and the door swings away on the opposite side.
The stones came shrink wrapped and dusty, and the manual says nothing about washing them.
Should the stones be rinsed before they ever go into the basket?

a: With the front panel at thirty-four, the running total there becomes one hundred fourteen kilograms.
The two short panels lift the figure to one hundred sixty-four on the corrected list.
The gable closes the list at one hundred eighty-four kilograms for all six panels.
That sits under the trailer rating of two hundred with sixteen kilograms to spare.
Is sixteen kilograms of margin enough to add the box of fixings to the same trip?
base: Rinse the stones in plain water and let them dry before they go anywhere near the basket.
Dust burned onto stone is the smell people blame on the timber for years afterward.
Stack them loosely around the heater so air can move between them instead of packing them tight.
The big stones sit low and the small ones ride near the top of the basket.
How many trial firings does the manual ask for before the first proper session?

a: Now lay out the build schedule, with the floor frame first thing on Saturday morning.
The frame takes one hour, each wall panel takes thirty minutes, and the roof takes two hours.
Work runs from eight in the morning with a half hour break at noon.
Give the clock time when the roof is finished if nothing overruns on the day.
Which panel is being fixed when the clock reaches half past ten?
base: The manual asks for three short trial firings before anyone sits in the heat properly.
We can run those on weekday evenings once the roof and the flue are done.
The benches worry me more, because the kit gives one height and my father is tall.
The top bench sits at one metre, and the ceiling is barely two metres above the floor.
Is there any room to raise that top bench without cooking whoever sits up there?

a: The floor frame runs from eight until nine, and the first wall panel follows straight after.
The six wall panels carry the work from nine until noon, one every thirty minutes.
At half past ten the fourth panel is going up, with three already fixed.
After the half hour break, the roof runs from half past twelve until half past two.
Does a finish at half past two leave enough light for felting the roof the same day?
base: Leave the top bench where the kit puts it, because heat stacks hard in a low room.
A tall sitter loses headroom, but raising the bench moves his head into the hottest layer.
Give him the lower bench on the first few sessions and see how he finds it.
Air matters more than height, so keep the gap under the door clear of flooring.
Did the kit include a vent slide for the wall opposite the door?

a: Print a short list of the four Sunday jobs in order for the helper.
Job one is the roof felt, job two is the door, and job three is the benches.
Job four is the trims, and every job needs its start time written beside it.
Sunday work begins at nine and each job takes ninety minutes with no breaks planned.
Which clock time starts the benches if the first two jobs run to plan?
base: There is a vent slide in the fittings box, still taped to the hinge pack.
We will fit it opposite the door and keep the gap under the door clear.
The trial firings are booked for three evenings, starting low and climbing a little each time.
My father has agreed to start on the lower bench without any argument at all.
Is there anything on the first firing that catches people out in a new room?

a: The roof felt runs from nine until half past ten on the Sunday list.
The door follows from half past ten until noon, and the benches start at noon exactly.
The benches run until half past one, and the trims close the day at three.
Every start time now sits beside its job on the printed list for the helper.
The build ends with the trims fixed, and the whole kit stands finished by three o'clock.
base: New rooms all sweat their first firing, so expect drips from the ceiling and wipe them down.
Keep the first fire small, prop the door open a hand's width, and let the timber dry slowly.
The smell of warm resin is normal for the first few evenings and then it fades.
Check the flue joint above the roof after the fire is out and fully cold.
After the third firing, close the door, warm it properly, and enjoy the first quiet hour.
